whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Energy & Utilities Accredited Professional exam for?

personas.label: Utility industry implementation consultants
personas.description: You deliver Salesforce projects for electric, gas, or water utilities and need the credential to validate your expertise in the Energy & Utilities Cloud data model and customer engagement workflows.

personas.label: Salesforce admins at utility companies
personas.description: You manage an Energy & Utilities Cloud org and want to prove your knowledge of service points, premises, meter-to-cash processes, and outage management.

personas.label: OmniStudio and integration partners
personas.description: You design customer journeys and billing system integrations for utility companies using OmniStudio and need to demonstrate your configuration skills.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Energy & Utilities Accredited Professional Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: The Energy & Utilities AP exam is moderately difficult. It tests utility-specific concepts including the service point data model, OmniStudio-powered customer journeys, meter-to-cash workflows, and billing system integration. Candidates without exposure to utility industry operations will find the domain terminology and regulatory context challenging.
bullets: ~65% passing score: roughly 39 correct answers needed.
Industry-specific data model: you must understand premises, service points, meters, and how customer billing accounts relate to physical service locations.
OmniStudio and integration knowledge: questions cover OmniScripts for start/stop service, FlexCards for agent consoles, and integration patterns with external billing systems like SAP IS-U.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Score 75%+ on practice exams and ensure you can explain the relationship between accounts, premises, service points, and meters before booking. Experience with at least one utility industry Salesforce implementation or familiarity with meter-to-cash processes is strongly recommended.

examFormat.heading: Energy & Utilities Accredited Professional Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: The exam is proctored online or in-person. Here is the format:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: About 40-50% of questions are scenario-based. Common patterns include configuring the service point hierarchy for a multi-premise customer, designing OmniScript-powered start/stop service workflows, and selecting the right integration approach for billing data from external systems.
bestWayToPass: Master the E&U data model: Know accounts, premises, service points, meters, and service orders. Understand the one-to-many relationships between customers, locations, and meter connections.
Understand OmniStudio components: Study how OmniScripts handle start service, move in/move out, and outage reporting. Know how FlexCards surface account balances and service order status.

Learn billing integration patterns: Know how billing data (balances, usage, payment history) flows from external billing systems into Salesforce, and how service requests flow back to the billing system.
Study Field Service integration: Understand how service orders trigger work orders in Field Service for meter installation, disconnect/connect, and fault repair dispatched to field crews.

certificationCard.description: This exam covers the Energy & Utilities Cloud data model, including service points, premises, and meter-to-cash processes. You’ll need to understand OmniStudio-powered customer journeys, outage management, and billing system integration.

keyConcepts.h2: Energy and Utilities Cloud: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Energy & Utilities Cloud Data Model
blocks.body: Energy & Utilities Cloud (EUC) provides an industry-specific data model for energy providers. Core objects: Account (residential or commercial customer), Premise (the physical service location, address where energy is delivered), Service Point (the meter connection at a premise), Asset (the meter or equipment), Service Order (a field work request, connect, disconnect, meter reading). The consultant understands how customer billing accounts relate to premises and service points in a one-to-many hierarchy, as a single customer may have multiple premises.

blocks.heading: OmniStudio-Powered Customer Journeys
blocks.body: Energy & Utilities Cloud uses OmniStudio (FlexCards and OmniScripts) extensively for customer-facing and agent-facing processes. Common OmniScripts: Start Service (new customer onboarding with service point activation), Move In/Move Out (transfer service to a new address), Outage Reporting (customer self-service outage notification). FlexCards surface account balance, recent bills, and active service orders in the customer and agent consoles. The consultant configures pre-built industry OmniStudio components and extends them to match the utility's specific business rules.

blocks.heading: Field Service Integration
blocks.body: Energy & Utilities Cloud integrates with Field Service to manage field crew dispatch for service orders (meter installation, disconnect, connect, fault repair). Work Orders created from Service Orders are scheduled and dispatched to field crews using FSL's scheduling optimisation. Mobile field workers use the FSL Mobile app to complete work orders and update service point status. The consultant designs the integration between EUC service order management and FSL scheduling, ensuring data flows correctly between the customer service and field operations processes.

blocks.heading: Customer Portal and Self-Service
blocks.body: Experience Cloud provides the customer-facing portal for energy utility customers. Self-service capabilities: view bills and payment history, make payments, report outages, start/stop/transfer service, manage account preferences. **Knowledge articles** address common questions (how to read your meter, what to do during an outage). The consultant configures the Experience Cloud site for utility customers, balancing self-service capabilities with the utility's compliance requirements around data access and service request validation.

blocks.heading: Billing Integration and Account Management
blocks.body: Utility billing systems (SAP IS-U, Oracle CC&B, Avertra) are external to Salesforce: Energy & Utilities Cloud serves as the CRM and customer engagement layer, not the billing system of record. Integration patterns: billing data (current balance, payment history, usage) syncs from the billing system to Salesforce via API or batch. Service requests flow from Salesforce to the billing system to activate or terminate service. The consultant designs the integration architecture, which data to sync, how frequently, and how to handle sync conflicts between systems.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Energy & Utilities Accredited Professional Exam
scenarioTips.intro: The Energy & Utilities AP exam tests Salesforce implementation for utility companies. Focus on the Energy & Utilities data model, service point management, and how the Industries platform addresses utility-specific business processes.

blocks.heading: Energy & Utilities Data Model
blocks.body: Know the key objects: Service Point (physical connection), Service Account (billing relationship), Premise (physical address), Meter, and how they relate to standard Account and Contact records.

blocks.heading: Customer Service for Utilities
blocks.body: Know how to configure utility-specific service requests: start/stop service, high bill inquiries, outage reporting, and how these map to Case types in Service Cloud with utility-specific case processes.

blocks.heading: Asset Management
blocks.body: Know how Salesforce Assets track utility infrastructure: meters, transformers, poles, and how the asset maintenance schedule integrates with Field Service for preventive maintenance work orders.

blocks.heading: Billing & Revenue
blocks.body: Know how utility billing integrates with Salesforce: smart meter data ingestion, usage-based billing calculations, time-of-use rate plans, and how Salesforce Revenue Cloud handles utility billing scenarios.

blocks.heading: Industry-Specific Analytics
blocks.body: Know the utility KPIs tracked in [CRM Analytics](/certifications/crm-analytics-einstein-discovery-consultant): customer satisfaction, outage metrics, service request volumes, energy efficiency program adoption, and how predictive analytics identifies at-risk customers.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Certifications After This AP
nextCertsAfter.intro: AP credentials pair well with core platform certifications. Consider:

sampleQuestions.question: A utility needs to hold both the person who pays the bill and the physical property being supplied. How is this modelled?
options: Two separate customer accounts, one for the payer and one for the property
A single account record holding the supply address in its own address fields
A contact record for the payer with the property stored as a related note
A customer account linked to a service point
sampleQuestions.explanation: The payer and the point of supply are different things, so the service point represents the premise and links to the account that pays for it.
whyWrong: Duplicating the account conflates a person with a place.
Address fields cannot represent a premise that outlives any one occupier.
A note is unstructured and cannot be reported on or billed against.

sampleQuestions.question: What does a service point represent in Energy and Utilities Cloud?
options: The meter reading taken at the end of each billing period for that address
The physical location where supply is delivered
The engineer appointment booked to attend the property for an inspection
The tariff that has been agreed with the customer for the current contract
sampleQuestions.explanation: A service point is the premise or delivery point itself, which persists even as occupiers, meters and tariffs change.
whyWrong: Readings are recorded against the service point rather than being it.
Appointments are work management records.
Tariffs are commercial terms attached to the contract.

sampleQuestions.question: A customer moves out and a new occupier moves in at the same address. What should happen?
options: The service point stays and the account link changes
Both occupiers are linked to the service point permanently for audit reasons
The service point is deleted and a new one created for the new occupier
A duplicate service point is created so each occupier has their own record
sampleQuestions.explanation: The premise does not change when the occupier does, so the service point persists and its relationship to the paying account is updated.
whyWrong: An open-ended link to a former occupier would keep billing them.
Deleting the service point loses the supply history for that address.
Duplicate service points for one address break consumption reporting.

sampleQuestions.question: Why does a utility usually need interval or usage data rather than a single monthly figure?
options: Billing systems are unable to process a single total for a whole month
Monthly figures cannot be stored in Salesforce without custom development work
Regulators require every reading to be published publicly within thirty days
Tariffs and demand vary by time of day
sampleQuestions.explanation: Time-of-use tariffs and demand charges depend on when energy was used, which a single monthly total cannot express.
whyWrong: Monthly totals are processable; they are just less useful.
Monthly totals are perfectly storable; the issue is what they can tell you.
Publication of individual readings is not a general requirement.

sampleQuestions.question: A customer disputes a bill and says the reading is wrong. What is the appropriate first step?
options: Issue a full credit note for the disputed bill and close the case immediately
Send an engineer to replace the meter at the property before investigating
Check the reading history for the service point
Move the customer onto a different tariff to reduce the amount they owe
sampleQuestions.explanation: The reading history shows whether the figure is consistent with past consumption, which is what tells you if there is a genuine problem.
whyWrong: Crediting before investigating gives away revenue without establishing cause.
Replacing hardware is expensive and premature before checking the data.
Changing tariff does not address whether the reading was correct.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of a usage profile?
options: It describes a typical pattern of consumption
It lists the appliances the customer has declared as installed on the premise
It stores the credit score used to decide whether to offer a payment plan
It records every complaint the customer has raised over the last four years
sampleQuestions.explanation: Usage profiles describe expected consumption patterns, which support estimating, forecasting and spotting anomalies.
whyWrong: Appliance inventories are not what a usage profile is for.
Credit assessment is a separate commercial process.
Complaint history is case management rather than usage.

sampleQuestions.question: A commercial customer has twelve sites on one contract. How should this be set up?
options: One contract with the twelve addresses listed in a long text description
Twelve separate contracts, each one covering a single site and its supply
One contract covering twelve service points
Twelve customer accounts, each holding one site and its own contract terms
sampleQuestions.explanation: A contract can cover many service points, which is what lets a single commercial agreement span multiple sites.
whyWrong: Addresses in free text cannot be billed or reported against.
Separate contracts per site lose the single commercial agreement.
Splitting the customer into twelve accounts fragments the relationship.

sampleQuestions.question: What distinguishes a regulated from a deregulated market in this context?
options: Whether the customer can choose their supplier
Whether the utility is permitted to store customer data inside Salesforce
Whether the utility supplies electricity only or both electricity and gas
Whether meter readings are taken monthly or on a quarterly basis instead
sampleQuestions.explanation: Deregulated markets let customers choose a retail supplier, which changes the processes a utility needs for switching and enrolment.
whyWrong: Data residency is a separate legal question.
The commodities supplied are unrelated to regulation.
Reading frequency is an operational choice, not the market structure.

sampleQuestions.question: A customer asks to spread their annual bill evenly across twelve months. What supports this?
options: A new contract backdated to the start of the current financial year instead
A separate service point created to carry the fixed monthly instalments
A credit note issued each month for the difference against actual usage
A budget or levelised payment plan
sampleQuestions.explanation: Budget plans charge a level amount each month and reconcile against actual consumption periodically.
whyWrong: Backdating a contract does not change how the customer pays.
Service points represent premises, not payment arrangements.
Monthly credit notes would misstate what the customer actually owes.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the main reason to integrate with a meter data management system?
options: It stores the customer's contact preferences and marketing consent records
It is the system of record for readings
It is the only system permitted by regulators to generate customer invoices
It manages the engineers and vehicles used for field service appointments
sampleQuestions.explanation: Meter data management holds and validates the readings, so Salesforce consumes that data rather than owning it.
whyWrong: Consent and preferences live with the customer record.
Invoicing is done by the billing system, not the meter data platform.
Field resources are managed in field service.

sampleQuestions.question: An agent needs to see consumption, billing and open cases for a customer on one screen. What achieves this?
options: A console layout bringing the related records together
A weekly report emailed to every agent covering all of their active customers
A nightly extract of the data into a spreadsheet the agent can search
A separate browser tab opened for each of the three systems involved
sampleQuestions.explanation: A console layout surfaces related records in context, which is what lets an agent answer a question without leaving the record.
whyWrong: A weekly report is stale by the time a customer calls.
A spreadsheet extract is neither current nor auditable.
Switching between systems slows every call and invites mistakes.

sampleQuestions.question: Why would a utility use asset records alongside service points?
options: To record the marketing campaigns a customer has responded to over time
To track the equipment installed at a premise
To store the tariff rates that apply to each of the supply points it serves
To hold the regulatory filings the utility submits at the end of each year
sampleQuestions.explanation: Assets represent the physical equipment, such as meters, installed at a premise, which can be replaced while the premise stays the same.
whyWrong: Campaign response belongs to marketing records.
Tariffs are commercial terms, not physical equipment.
Regulatory filings are documents, not installed assets.

sampleQuestions.question: A new housing development adds 400 premises. What is the efficient way to bring them in?
options: A single service point covering the whole development and its 400 premises
A bulk load of service points for the development
An individual case raised for each premise so an agent can create it by hand
A request to the meter data system asking it to create the records instead
sampleQuestions.explanation: Each premise needs its own service point, and 400 of them is a data load rather than a manual task.
whyWrong: One service point cannot represent 400 separately billed premises.
Manual creation of 400 records is slow and inconsistent.
The meter data system does not own the Salesforce service point records.

sampleQuestions.question: What does a work order typically represent for a utility?
options: The pattern of consumption expected at the premise over the coming year
The monthly invoice raised against the customer for their energy consumption
A job to be carried out at a premise
The contract the customer signed when they first took up the supply
sampleQuestions.explanation: Work orders capture jobs such as installations, reads and repairs, and link to the service point where the work happens.
whyWrong: Expected consumption is a usage profile.
Invoices are billing records.
Contracts are commercial agreements.

sampleQuestions.question: Which is the strongest argument for modelling premise and customer separately from the start?
options: It allows the utility to avoid integrating with the meter data system
It means tariffs no longer need to be attached to any contract record
Premises outlast the customers who occupy them
It reduces the number of records that have to be stored in the database
sampleQuestions.explanation: Supply history belongs to the address, and occupiers come and go, so separating them is what keeps consumption history intact across moves.
whyWrong: Meter data integration is needed regardless of the model.
Tariffs still attach to contracts either way.
Separating the model adds records rather than reducing them.
